# Abstract

Between the defeat of the Chanka confederation at Cusco around 1438AD and the arrival of Spanish forces at Cajamarca in 1532AD, the Inca state forged the largest indigenous polity of the Americas across 2,02M km² (2.019.488,2 km²) of Andean cordillera, Pacific littoral, altiplano and Amazonian piedmont. Across its five canonical territorial divisions - the Cusco imperial heartland plus the four quarters of Chinchaysuyu, Antisuyu, Cuntisuyu (Contisuyu) and Qullasuyu (Collasuyu) - aggregate population inside imperial borders expanded more than sevenfold from 1,24M (1.240.000) in 1438AD to 5,2M in 1470AD, 8,2M in 1500AD and a demographic peak of 9,45M (within a scholarly debate spanning 6M to 14M) around 1525AD on the eve of Old World epidemic contagion and dynastic civil war, before contracting by 11,75% to 8,34M at 1532AD [@bauer2004ancient; @covey2006how; @hyslop1990inka; @julien2009reading]. Imperial consolidation rested on decimal census accounting recorded on knotted *khipu* cords, rotational *mit'a* labour conscription, state-directed *mitmaqkuna* population transfers across ecological tiers and an arterial *Qhapaq Ñan* road system linking royal palaces, *tambo* waystations and provincial *llactas* from Ipiales on the Ancasmayo river to the Maipo and Maule valleys of central Chile [@murra1986expansion; @r2021multidisciplinary; @humphreys1986huanuco; @bernalvelez2020limites]. By 1532AD, demographic gravity remained markedly asymmetric: Chinchaysuyu held 3,95M inhabitants (47,36% of the empire at 6,73 inhabitants per km²) and Qullasuyu 2,78M (33,33% across 1,08M km² at 2,56 inhabitants per km²), while the compact Cusco heartland packed 460k residents into 5.511,6 km² at 83,46 inhabitants per km² and sustained an imperial capital of 145k people [@howlandrowe1985constitucion; @mr2025trees; @kosiba2022kevin]. This study reconciles sub-regional headcounts against decimal administrative units, provincial settlement archaeology and a gazetteer of 109 habitation sites spanning six modern Andean republics.

# Background

## Cusco State Formation and the Imperial Heartland

Tawantinsuyu - literally the "Four Parts Together" in Quechua - emerged in the first half of the fifteenth century out of a crowded landscape of competing chiefdoms in the southern Peruvian highlands [@bauer2004ancient; @covey2006how]. Before 1438AD, the Inca polity was a modest valley confederation centred on the Cusco basin, hemmed in by the Ayarmaca, Pinagua and Muyna polities to the north and east and by the expanding Chanka confederation across the Apurímac river to the west.

Archaeological survey across more than 1.000 km² of the Cusco region demonstrates that state consolidation began well before the traditional imperial horizon through agricultural intensification, canal building and selective alliance formation along the Vilcanota-Urubamba corridor [@covey2006how; @mr2025trees]. Yet it was the crisis of the Chanka invasion and the accession of Pachakuti Inka Yupanki around 1438AD that transformed a regional valley chiefdom into an expansionist bureaucratic empire [@julien2009reading; @howlandrowe1985constitucion].

Pachakuti and his successors Thupa Inka Yupanki (c. 1471AD to 1493AD) and Wayna Qhapaq (c. 1493AD to 1527AD) organised the expanding realm into a radial geometry anchored on the Hawkaypata plaza and the Coricancha temple of Cusco [@howlandrowe1985constitucion; @ziokowski2018astronomical]. Four great quarters (*suyus*) radiated outward from the capital, each governed by an *apu* sitting on the imperial council alongside the *panaca* royal descent groups and non-Inca aristocratic lineages of upper (*Hanan*) and lower (*Hurin*) Cusco [@howlandrowe1985constitucion; @kosiba2022kevin].

At the centre lay the Cusco Imperial Heartland itself, a compact 5.511,6 km² core encompassing the Cusco urban basin, the Anta plain of Jaquijahuana, the Sacred Valley royal estates of Yucay, Pisac, Calca and Ollantaytambo, the experimental agricultural terraces of Moray and the southern gateway at Rumicolca [@ayala2024legacy; @mr2025trees; @bauer2004ancient]. Around 1438AD, this core already held 320k inhabitants at 58,06 persons per km², rising to 520k at 94,35 persons per km² by 1525AD as royal estates drew thousands of *yanakuna* retainers, artisans and ceremonial specialists from distant provinces [@l2023insights; @covey2006how].

## Chinchaysuyu: The Populous Northern Highway

Chinchaysuyu stretched northwestward from the Apurímac river through the central Peruvian sierra, the densely irrigated north coast valleys and the Ecuadorian intermontane basins as far as the Ancasmayo river in southern Colombia [@hyslop1990inka; @bernalvelez2020limites]. Geographically it represented only 29,05% of the empire's 1532AD surface (586.590,5 km²), yet it contained nearly half of all imperial subjects because it absorbed the richest pre-Inca agrarian and urban polities of the Andes.

Those conquered realms included the Wanka of the Mantaro valley, the coastal states of Chincha, Ichma and Chimor, the highland kingdoms of Cajamarca and Huamachuco and the Cañari, Puruhá and Caranqui-Cayambe confederations of Ecuador [@murra1986expansion; @humphreys1986huanuco; @jl2026ancient]. Rather than flattening local agrarian infrastructure, imperial administrators grafted state farms, *qollqa* storehouses and provincial garrisons onto existing valley irrigation networks.

Imperial control in Chinchaysuyu depended on newly founded highland administrative *llactas* laid out along the trunk *Qhapaq Ñan* road. Hatun Xauxa (32,4k at 1530AD), Pumpu (11,4k), Huánuco Pampa (18,4k), Huamachuco (11,2k) and Cajamarca (27,6k) functioned as vast logistical plazas surrounded by hundreds of hillside storehouses capable of provisioning marching armies of 30k to 50k men [@humphreys1986huanuco; @murra1986expansion].

On the Pacific coast, Inca rule adapted existing urban monuments rather than erasing them. At Chan Chan Inca (36,4k in 1470AD falling to 19,6k by 1530AD after Chimú political dismantling), Farfán Inca (9,18k), Túcume Inca (18,6k), Pachacamac Inca (29,8k) and Chincha Inca (28,2k), Cusco governed through co-opted local *kurakas* while constructing smaller adobe garrisons such as Tambo Colorado (6,14k) and Inkawasi Lunahuaná [@hyslop1990inka; @jl2026ancient].

Farther north, prolonged warfare against the Caranqui and Pasto confederations under Wayna Qhapaq produced a dense frontier infrastructure of mountain fortresses (*pukaras*) around Pambamarca (4,28k) and Cochasquí [@bernalvelez2020limites; @kosiba2022kevin]. Behind that defensive ring rose a second imperial capital at Tomebamba (46,8k) in Cañari territory, a major northern hub at Quito (44,6k) and terminal border garrisons at Caranqui Inca (13,4k) and Ipiales Ancasmayo (5,34k) [@bernalvelez2020limites; @hyslop1990inka].

## Qullasuyu: Altiplano Kingdoms, Mines and the Southern Frontier

Qullasuyu (spelled Collasuyu in early colonial Spanish chronicles and in the regional tables below) was by far the largest quarter of Tawantinsuyu, covering 1.084.732,6 km² or 53,71% of the entire empire [@hyslop1990inka; @garcia2021radiocarbon]. Beginning immediately southeast of Cusco at Raqch'i (5,68k) in the Vilcanota valley, it encompassed the high-altitude Lake Titicaca basin, the Bolivian altiplano, the silver districts of Porco (9,24k) and Potosí, the valleys of Salta, Jujuy, Tucumán and Catamarca in northwestern Argentina, the Atacama oasis chain and central Chile southward to the Maipo and Maule rivers [@otero2022analisis; @lynch2012aproximacion; @manriquezsoto1999termino].

Because much of this expanse consisted of arid *puna*, salt flats and high steppe above 3.800 metres, regional density remained low - 2,56 inhabitants per km² in 1532AD - yet the shorelands of Lake Titicaca formed one of the empire's densest agro-pastoral reservoirs. Around the lake, the Lupaqa and Qulla polities had sustained large populations on raised-field agriculture, freeze-dried *chuño* tubers and immense llama and alpaca herds long before Inca annexation [@murra1986expansion; @julien2009reading].

Under Cusco rule, Hatuncolla Inca (21,6k), Chucuito Inca (25,4k), Paucarcolla, Juli (12,2k), Pomata and Copacabana (11,4k) became major administrative centres and pilgrimage stations along the twin highways skirting the eastern and western shores of Lake Titicaca [@julien2009reading; @hyslop1990inka]. South of the altiplano, imperial expansion between roughly 1470AD and 1490AD pushed down the Quebrada de Humahuaca and the Calchaquí valleys into northwestern Argentina and across the cordillera into Chile [@garcia2021radiocarbon; @cremonte2012espacios].

Rather than building huge cities in the southern valleys, Inca engineers established spaced ceremonial, pastoral and metallurgical hubs: Tilcara Inca (6,72k) and La Paya (4,56k) along the Humahuaca and Calchaquí corridors [@otero2022analisis; @cremonte2012espacios], Hualfín Inka and El Shincal de Quimivil (6,84k) in Catamarca [@lynch2012aproximacion; @giovanetti2021chakana; @moralejo2020evaluacion], Caspana, Catarpe (5,12k) and Turi (3,96k) in the Atacama oases [@manriquezsoto1999termino; @jorquerasilva2021estado] and Quillota Aconcagua (7,92k) and Mapocho (9,68k) in central Chile. High-altitude mining at Abra de Minas and Cueva Inca Viejo in Salta operated alongside *qhapaq hucha* summit sanctuaries across the southern Andes [@lopez2020ocupacion; @c2024genomic].

## Cuntisuyu and Antisuyu: Pacific Valleys and the Montaña Edge

Cuntisuyu (Contisuyu) and Antisuyu formed the smaller transverse wings of the empire, balancing the long north-south spine of Chinchaysuyu and Qullasuyu. Cuntisuyu covered 147.720,2 km² (7,31% of the domain) across the rugged volcanic highlands and steep desert canyons draining southwestern Peru toward the Pacific between Nazca, Arequipa and Tacna [@hyslop1990inka; @howlandrowe1985constitucion].

Its highland crossroads at Vilcashuamán (19,8k) and Andahuaylas (11,6k) linked Cusco to the coastal plains, while terraced valley centres at Maucallacta (5,42k), Chuquibamba, Cotahuasi and Arequipa Yanahuara (10,6k) sustained irrigated maize and cotton production, backed by coastal storage complexes at Paredones Nazca, Quebrada de la Vaca and Camaná Inca [@mr2025trees; @ayala2024legacy].

Antisuyu occupied 194.933,3 km² (9,65% of imperial territory) along the steep eastern escarpment of the Andes, descending from cloud-forest ridges (*ceja de selva*) into humid coca-growing *yungas* and the Bolivian foothills [@kauffmanndoig2014machu; @astetevictoria2017inca]. On the upper Urubamba approach, royal sanctuaries and agricultural complexes such as Machu Picchu (1,12k), Patallacta Llactapata, Wiñay Wayna (540) and the astronomical observatory at Inkaraqay anchored frontier ritual geography without attempting deep lowland conquest [@astetevictoria2017inca; @kauffmanndoig2014machu; @l2023insights].

Farther south in the Bolivian *montaña* and Cochabamba valleys, however, Antisuyu acquired major strategic and demographic weight. Wayna Qhapaq transformed the Cochabamba basin into an imperial maize granary worked by up to 14k *mitmaqkuna* colonists from across the altiplano, centred on Cotapachi Cochabamba (26,8k), alongside eastern fortified complexes at Inkallajta (5,94k) and Samaipata (4,78k) guarding the Chiriguano frontier [@r2021multidisciplinary; @murra1986expansion].

## Decimal Administration, *Mit'a*, *Mitmaqkuna* and the Road System

What enabled a single highland capital to extract surpluses from 6M to 14M subjects across 40 degrees of latitude without wheeled transport or alphabetic script was an integrated administrative triad: decimal *khipu* enumeration, rotational *mit'a* labour service and compulsory *mitmaqkuna* resettlement [@julien2009reading; @r2021multidisciplinary; @murra1986expansion]. State officials periodically surveyed provincial populations and grouped households into nested decimal tiers - *pachaka* (100 households), *waranqa* (1.000) and *hunu* (10.000) - recording tribute obligations, demographic age grades and agricultural stores on dyed cotton or camelid-fibre *khipus* [@julien2009reading; @howlandrowe1985constitucion].

Rather than levying coin taxes, the Crown collected labour-days (*mit'a*) from subject households for road maintenance, terrace construction, state-farm cultivation, textile weaving, mining and military campaigns [@murra1986expansion; @mr2025trees; @lopez2020ocupacion]. To break provincial solidarity and colonise underused ecological niches, Inca rulers uprooted entire communities as *mitmaqkuna* and dispatched them hundreds or thousands of kilometres from their homelands [@r2021multidisciplinary].

Recent ancient DNA and strontium-isotope studies confirm the demographic reach of this policy: retainers buried at Machu Picchu carried genetic ancestry spanning the Peruvian coast, the northern highlands and the Amazonian rim [@l2023insights], while *qhapaq hucha* sanctuaries and coastal ossuary populations document long-distance movement across distant ecological zones [@c2024genomic; @jl2026ancient]. Binding these dispersed colonies together was the *Qhapaq Ñan*, a paved and stepped highway network exceeding 30.000 km with suspension bridges and *tambo* waystations spaced every 15 to 25 km, allowing *chaski* runners and armies to traverse the empire rapidly [@bernalvelez2020limites; @moralejo2020evaluacion].

# Methodology

## Pre-Contact Andean Population Debates: 6M to 14M

Modern historical demography of Tawantinsuyu has revolved for eight decades around a sharp divergence between low-count institutional estimates and high-count epidemic back-projections [@julien2009reading; @bauer2004ancient; @murra1986expansion]. Early conservative syntheses by John Howland Rowe and Angel Rosenblat anchored Inca population near 4M to 6M on the basis of early Spanish provincial counts (*visitas*) compiled in the 1560s and 1570s under Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, assuming modest pre-Toledan mortality between 1532AD and 1570AD [@howlandrowe1985constitucion; @julien2009reading].

Subsequent regional work in the 1960s and 1970s by Noble David Cook, Nathan Wachtel and Henry Dobyns showed that Old World smallpox, measles and influenza struck the Andes in successive waves starting around 1524AD to 1526AD - even before Pizarro landed at Tumbes - and accelerated sharply after 1532AD, implying depopulation ratios between 2:1 and 4:1 prior to Toledo's general census [@julien2009reading; @murra1986expansion].

Back-projection from Toledo's counted tribute population (roughly 1,3M to 1,5M in the core Viceroyalty of Peru, excluding peripheral Audiencia zones of Quito, Tucumán and Chile) across distinct regional mortality slopes produces a credible scholarly envelope between 6M and 14M for Tawantinsuyu at its pre-epidemic zenith around 1525AD [@bauer2004ancient; @kosiba2022kevin]. Estimates toward 12M to 14M assume severe early epidemic losses on the warm north coast and Ecuadorian lowlands alongside maximum carrying capacities for terraced highland valleys, whereas estimates near 6M to 7M discount early coastal mortality and assume smaller household multipliers per *hatun runa* taxpayer [@covey2006how; @mr2025trees].

Rather than adopting either extreme uncritically, our model calibrates each quarter independently from regional survey archaeology, known *hunu* and *waranqa* provincial groupings and ecological carrying capacity [@humphreys1986huanuco; @hyslop1990inka].

## Territorial Sub-Regions and Benchmark Chronology

To track demographic growth as Cusco expanded from a valley chiefdom to a continental empire, the 2.019.488,2 km² territory of Tawantinsuyu at maximum extent is partitioned into five spatially explicit polygons matching imperial political geography: Cusco Imperial Heartland (5.511,6 km²), Chinchaysuyu (586.590,5 km²), Qullasuyu or Collasuyu (1.084.732,6 km²), Cuntisuyu or Contisuyu (147.720,2 km²) and Antisuyu (194.933,3 km²).

Population is evaluated at five benchmark horizons chosen to capture both imperial annexation waves and the late pre-conquest demographic shock:

1. 1438AD: Victory over the Chankas and consolidation of the Cusco heartland plus early tributary spheres in adjacent valleys.
2. 1470AD: Completion of Pachakuti's campaigns across the Titicaca basin, central highlands and Cuntisuyu, alongside Thupa Inka Yupanki's conquest of Chimor on the north coast.
3. 1500AD: Consolidation of southern Qullasuyu (northwestern Argentina, Atacama and central Chile) and expansion into southern Ecuador and the Cochabamba granaries [@garcia2021radiocarbon; @r2021multidisciplinary].
4. 1525AD: Territorial and demographic apogee under Wayna Qhapaq just prior to the northern smallpox epidemic and the succession crisis between Huascar and Atahualpa.
5. 1532AD: Arrival of Spanish forces at Cajamarca after initial epidemic mortality in Chinchaysuyu and coastal valleys combined with fratricidal war losses across Ecuador and the central sierra [@julien2009reading; @murra1986expansion].

## Reconciling Regional Totals with Imperial Expansion

Note carefully what the time-series represents. At 1438AD, the five sub-regional figures reflect the pre-imperial and early Inca baseline within each territorial footprint that would subsequently comprise Tawantinsuyu (1,24M total within the active early Cusco-led sphere, dominated by 320k in the Cusco heartland and 450k in immediately adjacent central-Andean valleys of Chinchaysuyu).

By 1470AD, as imperial conquest incorporated the north coast and altiplano, the counted imperial population surged to 5,2M. Further annexation into Ecuador, Argentina and Chile carried the empire to 8,2M in 1500AD and to its peak of 9,45M in 1525AD - squarely in the centre of the 6M to 14M historiographical range [@bauer2004ancient; @kosiba2022kevin].

Between 1525AD and 1532AD, the first Old World contagion and the Huascar-Atahualpa civil war reduced aggregate population by 1,11M (-11,75%) to 8,34M, falling hardest on Chinchaysuyu (-650k, from 4,6M to 3,95M) where dense coastal valleys and northern war zones suffered simultaneously [@murra1986expansion; @jl2026ancient].

## Settlement Gazetteer Construction

Alongside the five regional time-series, a gazetteer of 109 imperial settlements was compiled across Peru (62 sites), Bolivia (13), Ecuador (12), Argentina (11), Chile (10) and Colombia (1) [@bernalvelez2020limites; @garcia2021radiocarbon; @manriquezsoto1999termino]. Every site is anchored to WGS84 coordinates, assigned to one of the five sub-regions and linked to primary archaeological monographs and national heritage inventories.

Peak settlement populations are calibrated from architectural footprint, *kancha* residential compound counts, *qollqa* storage capacity and early colonial *tasa* tributary accounts rather than uniform site-tier multipliers [@humphreys1986huanuco; @ayala2024legacy; @giovanetti2021chakana].

# Testing and Validation

Cross-validation of the Tawantinsuyu demographic model rests on three independent checks: internal reconciliation between the gridded mask and vector sub-regions, architectural and storage calibration of provincial *llactas* and chronological testing against radiocarbon series along imperial frontiers.

First, area and population accounting across the vector sub-regions and the 4.320 by 2.160 gridded surface matches within 0,36%: the vector summary spans 2.019.488,2 km² compared with 2.012.249 km² across 24.996 occupied grid cells, while all five sub-regions sum cleanly to 1,24M (1438AD), 5,2M (1470AD), 8,2M (1500AD), 9,45M (1525AD) and 8,34M (1532AD). Uncertainty bounds around every benchmark total and regional series follow asymmetric pre-industrial calibration intervals of plus or minus 25% for early expansion horizons (1438AD and 1470AD) and plus or minus 22% for the late imperial horizons (1500AD, 1525AD and 1532AD), yielding a 1525AD interval of 7,37M to 11,53M and a 1532AD interval of 6,51M to 10,17M.

Second, urban and provincial estimates were tested against archaeological site plans and *qollqa* capacities [@humphreys1986huanuco; @hyslop1990inka; @moralejo2020evaluacion]. At Huánuco Pampa, Morris and Thompson's excavation of roughly 4.000 structures and 497 *qollqa* storehouses (approximately 38.000 cubic metres of storage) supports a resident and rotating *mit'a* population around 18,4k at 1530AD, consistent with its rank below major demographic valleys such as Hatun Xauxa (32,4k) and Tomebamba (46,8k) [@humphreys1986huanuco]. Similarly, Bauer's intensive pedestrian survey of Cusco and its surrounding valley supports an imperial metropolis of 145k inhabitants across the urban core and immediate suburban parishes by 1530AD [@bauer2004ancient; @covey2006how].

Third, expansion chronology was tested against Bayesian radiocarbon analyses in peripheral provinces. In northwestern and central-west Argentina, 108 radiocarbon determinations compiled by García, Moralejo and Ochoa confirm Inca presence beginning around 1400AD to 1470AD and peaking in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, justifying our 1470AD to 1500AD inflection in southern Qullasuyu [@garcia2021radiocarbon; @lynch2012aproximacion]. Comparable chronological anchors at El Shincal de Quimivil, Tilcara Inca, Cueva Inca Viejo and northern sites near Ancasmayo confirm that imperial settlement networks reached full spatial extent well before 1525AD [@giovanetti2021chakana; @otero2022analisis; @lopez2020ocupacion; @bernalvelez2020limites].

# Results

## Sub-Regional Demographic Trajectory, 1438AD to 1532AD

Across the 94 years from the Chanka war to the Spanish landing, Tawantinsuyu experienced the fastest sustained state-driven demographic integration in pre-Columbian South American history. Table \ref{tab:subregion-pop} presents the full five-benchmark series across all five territorial divisions, while Figure \ref{fig:pop-trajectory} plots both the aggregate imperial trajectory and 1532AD sub-regional densities.

Three spatial patterns stand out clearly in the trajectory. First, Chinchaysuyu was throughout the imperial era the demographic engine of the state. Rising from 450k in 1438AD to 2,4M in 1470AD after the incorporation of the central sierra and Chimor, it reached 3,95M in 1500AD and 4,6M at its 1525AD apex (48,68% of all imperial subjects), sustaining 7,84 inhabitants per km² across a mountainous territory spanning coastal desert oases and Ecuadorian basins [@murra1986expansion; @humphreys1986huanuco]. Even after suffering the steepest contraction between 1525AD and 1532AD (-14,13% or -650k inhabitants under early smallpox and northern civil war devastation), Chinchaysuyu still accounted for 47,36% of the empire at 1532AD [@julien2009reading; @bernalvelez2020limites].

Second, Qullasuyu combined continental scale with stark internal concentration. Expanding from 280k in 1438AD to 1,65M in 1470AD, 2,65M in 1500AD and 3,05M in 1525AD (32,28% of the empire), it held 2,78M inhabitants at 1532AD after a milder 8,85% decline (-270k). Over its vast 1.084.732,6 km² extent, mean density averaged just 2,56 inhabitants per km², yet that figure conceals the dense Lupaqa and Qulla agricultural core around Lake Titicaca alongside sparsely settled Atacameño oases and southern mountain valleys in Catamarca, Mendoza and central Chile [@otero2022analisis; @cremonte2012espacios; @jorquerasilva2021estado; @garcia2021radiocarbon].

Third, the Cusco Imperial Heartland remained an extraordinary demographic outlier. Occupying only 0,27% of imperial territory (5.511,6 km²), the heartland held 320k residents in 1438AD, climbed steadily to 420k (1470AD), 480k (1500AD) and 520k (1525AD), and stood at 460k in 1532AD (5,52% of Tawantinsuyu). Its density of 83,46 inhabitants per km² in 1532AD (peaking at 94,35 in 1525AD) exceeded Chinchaysuyu more than twelvefold and Qullasuyu more than thirty-two-fold, sustained by engineered *andenes* terracing, canalised river valleys, agroforestry and state grain redistribution [@mr2025trees; @ayala2024legacy; @bauer2004ancient; @covey2006how].

Meanwhile, Cuntisuyu and Antisuyu contributed steady but smaller shares. Cuntisuyu rose from 110k in 1438AD to 760k in 1525AD before easing to 670k in 1532AD (8,03% of the empire, 4,54 inhabitants per km²), anchored by the terraced valleys of Arequipa, Cotahuasi and Vilcashuamán [@howlandrowe1985constitucion; @mr2025trees]. Antisuyu expanded from 80k in 1438AD to 520k in 1525AD and 480k in 1532AD (5,76% of the empire, 2,46 inhabitants per km²), boosted primarily by state-sponsored maize colonisation in Cochabamba and Chuquiabo alongside fortified *montaña* estates [@r2021multidisciplinary; @kauffmanndoig2014machu; @astetevictoria2017inca].

## Settlement Network and Urban Hierarchy

Imperial demographic concentration is mirrored cleanly in the urban and administrative hierarchy shown in Figure \ref{fig:urban-hierarchy} and summarised by sub-regional shares in Table \ref{tab:subregion-shares}. Across all 109 catalogued settlements, peak site populations span from 145k at Cusco down to 495 inhabitants at the small Uspallata waystation of Tambillos in Mendoza, with a median peak of 5.940 at Puruchuco on the central coast.

Log-log rank-size regression across the top half of the urban system produces a shallow power-law slope of $\alpha = 0,74$ ($R^2 = 0,98$), revealing an articulated administrative network rather than a single parasitic primate city. Cusco itself stood apart at 145k (more than three times larger than the second-ranking city), reflecting its status as ritual axis, court seat of twelve royal *panacas* and hub of four radiating *suyu* highways [@bauer2004ancient; @howlandrowe1985constitucion; @ziokowski2018astronomical]. Directly beneath Cusco stood two northern capitals in Ecuador - Tomebamba (46,8k) and Quito (44,6k) - built to project imperial power during the northern wars and nearly autonomous as a second royal court under Wayna Qhapaq [@hyslop1990inka; @kosiba2022kevin].

Below the northern dyad came an exceptionally balanced tier of coastal and highland provincial *llactas* between 18k and 37k inhabitants: Chan Chan Inca (36,4k in 1470AD, declining to 19,6k by 1530AD), Hatun Xauxa (32,4k), Pachacamac Inca (29,8k), Chincha Inca (28,2k), Cajamarca (27,6k), Cotapachi Cochabamba (26,8k), Chucuito Inca (25,4k), Hatuncolla Inca (21,6k), Vilcashuamán (19,8k), Armatambo Inca (18,9k), Túcume Inca (18,6k) and Huánuco Pampa (18,4k) [@humphreys1986huanuco; @hyslop1990inka].

Beneath these major centres lay more than eighty secondary *tambo* complexes, valley capitals, agricultural estates and frontier garrisons ranging from 14,6k at Chuquiabo and 13,4k at Caranqui Inca down through 5,94k at Inkallajta, 6,84k at El Shincal de Quimivil and 6,72k at Tilcara Inca to compact roadside waystations under 1k [@giovanetti2021chakana; @otero2022analisis; @lynch2012aproximacion; @moralejo2020evaluacion]. Below rank 60, the steep tail-off in Figure \ref{fig:urban-hierarchy} reflects the selective inclusion of excavated state *tambos* rather than every dispersed agrarian hamlet.

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties qualify demographic reconstruction for Tawantinsuyu. First, the empire lacked alphabetic census registers; while knotted *khipus* preserved precise decimal household counts at the *waranqa* and *hunu* levels, only fragments survived the conquest in early Spanish *visitas* and legal testimonies [@julien2009reading; @howlandrowe1985constitucion]. Consequently, all imperial totals remain bounded within the 6M to 14M historiographical bracket, and our 1525AD peak of 9,45M carries an explicit uncertainty margin of plus or minus 22% (7,37M to 11,53M).

Second, dating and magnitude of the pre-Pizarro epidemic remain imperfectly constrained. Chroniclers recorded a devastating pestilence - most likely smallpox, possibly compounded by measles - sweeping from the Caribbean and Panama down the northern Andes around 1524AD to 1527AD, claiming Wayna Qhapaq and his designated heir Ninan Cuyochi in Quito [@julien2009reading; @murra1986expansion]. Yet quantifying exactly whether mortality between 1525AD and 1532AD removed 10%, 15% or 25% of Chinchaysuyu's coastal and highland population cannot be resolved directly from archaeology alone, and skeletal ossuaries show complex multi-century demographic baselines predating contact [@jl2026ancient].

Third, Inca urban archaeology relies heavily on planned stone architecture and surface pottery, which disproportionately highlights state *llactas*, *tambos* and elite sanctuaries while under-representing dispersed rural hamlets built of perishable adobe or *quincha* reed walls [@ayala2024legacy; @jorquerasilva2021estado]. In Table \ref{tab:subregion-shares}, site density per 10.000 km² reaches 23,59 in the intensely surveyed Cusco heartland compared with just 0,31 across vast Qullasuyu and 0,62 in forested Antisuyu; rural population totals therefore derive from regional carrying capacities and *mit'a* province counts rather than naive summation of catalogued town populations [@mr2025trees; @covey2006how].

Fourth, *mitmaqkuna* resettlement complicates static spatial attribution [@r2021multidisciplinary]. Tens of thousands of colonists rotated seasonally or relocated permanently between highland *puna* homelands, coastal valleys and *montaña* maize estates such as Cochabamba, while retainers drawn from distant provinces lived permanently in royal estates around Cusco [@l2023insights; @c2024genomic]. Our sub-regional figures reflect resident populations within each territorial boundary at each benchmark rather than tracing ethnic origin across quarters.

# Conclusion

Between 1438AD and 1532AD, Tawantinsuyu accomplished the most rapid demographic and political integration of pre-Columbian South America. Starting from an active early Inca-centred sphere of 1,24M in 1438AD, successive conquests under Pachakuti, Thupa Inka Yupanki and Wayna Qhapaq built an empire of 2.019.488,2 km² uniting 5,2M people in 1470AD, 8,2M in 1500AD and 9,45M at its 1525AD zenith before early epidemic disease and dynastic civil war cut numbers to 8,34M by 1532AD [@bauer2004ancient; @julien2009reading; @murra1986expansion]. Even at 1532AD, the empire held roughly one person in five of the entire pre-contact Americas within a single decimal administrative system.

What gave Tawantinsuyu its enduring demographic resilience - and simultaneously created its vulnerability to Old World contagion - was the extreme connectivity of its highland-coastal spine [@hyslop1990inka; @r2021multidisciplinary]. While the compact Cusco heartland sustained 83,46 inhabitants per km² and Chinchaysuyu concentrated 3,95M subjects across irrigated valleys and intermontane basins, the *Qhapaq Ñan* highway, *tambo* network and *mitmaqkuna* colonies bound distant frontier provinces from Ancasmayo to the Maule into one logistical organism [@bernalvelez2020limites; @garcia2021radiocarbon; @manriquezsoto1999termino]. When European pathogens and steel arrived at Cajamarca in 1532AD, they struck an empire already weakened by a 1,11M demographic contraction and poised on the threshold of the catastrophic Andean collapse examined in the following chapter.

## National Distribution of Catalogued Settlements

Table \ref{tab:country-sites} aggregates the 109 catalogued Inca-era habitation sites across the six modern Andean states spanned by Tawantinsuyu.
